summary: LongJudgeBench consolidates six human-labelled long-form evaluation datasets (DeepResearch Bench, a new 640-document RealDeepResearch, SurGE surveys, WritingPreferenceBench, VerifyBench, clinical meta-analysis MA; average output >9,000 tokens) into one format with pointwise/pairwise/listwise protocols, and measures agreement of 8 LLM judges under vanilla, rubric, reference, and reference+rubric settings. Judges are unreliable: mean accuracy 0.5639 across 32 model-setting combinations, best 0.6744 (Qwen3-Max + reference).

claims.claim: Long-form LLM judging is far from solved: overall mean accuracy 0.5639, best 0.6744, only 12 of 32 configurations exceed 0.60.
claims.evidence: Table 3 (0.6744 present) and §5.1. Single temperature-0 run, no CIs. Compared against a 'random pairwise baseline of 0.5' but exact-match accuracy counts ties, and no human-human agreement ceiling is reported per dataset (DR-Bench source IAA is 68.44%, RealDR ICC_avg 0.76; App. C), so how far judges are from the achievable ceiling is unclear.

claims.claim: References help most on average (0.5334 -> 0.5866); rubrics help on multi-dimensional reports (DR-Bench 0.5479 -> 0.7075) but hurt on SurGE-Content and MA; Ref+Rubric (0.5786) is not additive.

Stronger general models are not necessarily better long-form judges (GPT-5.2 and GPT-4o-mini lower than Qwen3-Max/DeepSeek-V4-Flash/GLM-5.1); Qwen3-32B thinking mode lowers average (0.5762 -> 0.5253).
claims.evidence: Table 3; single run per configuration, GPT-5.2 configuration details (reasoning effort) not stated in §4.1.

claims.claim: The effect of output length on judge accuracy is dataset-specific, not simply 'longer is worse'.
claims.evidence: §5.2 Figure 2 quartile bins, 4 judges, vanilla setting.

claims.claim: Judges are misled by superficial coverage and domain concept confusion.
claims.evidence: §5.3 two case studies (e.g. Qwen3-Max 9.26 vs human 5.87) plus position-bias analysis in App. B; anecdotal for the qualitative part.

patterns.note: Direct evidence that LLM-as-judge on long documents agrees with humans only modestly (mean 0.56, best 0.67), with failures on medical-domain content; supports reference-anchored judging over vanilla.
Explicit rubrics (acceptance-criteria-like) help on structured report evaluation but can hurt elsewhere; references (expected outputs) help more consistently.
Meta-evaluation benchmark for judges rather than for agents.

methodology.sample: Six datasets across five scenarios; RealDeepResearch 640 docs (40 tasks x 4 prompt styles x 4 generators); SurGE 41 topics/164 surveys; DR-Bench 200 human-annotated Chinese reports; others sampled subsets (Table 2).
methodology.baselines: 8 judge models x 4 settings (32 combos); no specialised judge models (e.g. fine-tuned evaluators) or multi-agent judging (acknowledged in Limitations).
methodology.models: Qwen3-32B (with/without thinking), Qwen3-Max, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5.2, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6.
methodology.variance: Temperature 0, single run; no CIs or significance tests; pairwise orders swapped and averaged.
methodology.ablations: Judging setting (rubric/reference), thinking mode, output-length bins, position bias (App. B).
methodology.contamination_controls: None discussed; public source datasets may be seen by judge models.
methodology.languages: Chinese and English natural-language documents; no code outputs.

standards.artifacts: Code at github.com/cjj826/LongJudgeBench; prompts App. D; annotation guidelines App. F; dataset licenses App. A.

biases.detail: Single deterministic run per configuration; differences of 0.01-0.03 are not tested.
Accuracy against human labels is interpreted without per-dataset human agreement ceilings, so 'slightly above random' overstates judge failure where humans themselves agree ~68%.
RealDeepResearch built by authors and SurGE co-authored by a co-author (Su et al.); not a commercial COI.

coi.affiliations: Tsinghua University, Quancheng Laboratory, University of Science and Technology Beijing.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Third-party LLMs only; authors ship no top-ranked judge.
coi.detail: Academic benchmark; no product or ranked system of the authors.

verdict_reason: Peer-reviewed, well-documented benchmark with human-validated references (ICC 0.76 on the new set), many current judge models, and released code; headline numbers match Table 3. Caveats: single run without CIs, no human-ceiling comparison, natural-language documents only (no code or specs).
applicability: Directly relevant to any harness step that uses an LLM reviewer to grade long artifacts: generated specs, design docs, long-form summaries, or multi-file PR descriptions spanning the several repositories. Evidence says do not let an LLM judge be the sole gate on long-form outputs; anchor it with references (golden examples/expected outputs) more than with rubrics, keep deterministic checks (schema validation, contract tests, spec-conformance tests) as the hard gate, and route medical-domain content to human review (MA scored 0.4983). Judge choice should be measured on the team's own labelled samples rather than picked by general model strength, which matters with mixed agent hosts using different default models.

conflicts_with.detail: That paper treats a four-LLM judge ensemble as reliable for long tutorial-style documentation based on inter-judge agreement; LongJudgeBench shows long-form LLM judges agree with humans at only ~0.56 mean accuracy and fail on domain concepts, so judge-judge agreement does not establish validity.
TerminalBench-O grades long multimodal outputs with an LLM judge; LongJudgeBench's findings imply such scores need human-agreement validation.
